mcqs.question: The same function `whoAmI` is attached to two different objects and called as `alice.whoAmI()` and `bob.whoAmI()`, returning different results each time. Why?
options: `this` is resolved at the call site based on what's left of the dot, not fixed by the function's own definition
JavaScript automatically creates a separate copy of the function for each object it's attached to
The function's definition captures whichever object called it first
`this` defaults to the most recently created object in memory
mcqs.explanation: `this` binding is decided fresh at every call, from how the function is invoked — here, implicit binding via the object to the left of the dot. There's only one `whoAmI` function object shared by both, and nothing about the definition itself locks in a particular receiver.

mcqs.question: Given `const obj = { fn: function() {} }; new obj.fn();` — which binding rule decides `this` inside `fn`?
options: Implicit binding, because of the `obj.fn` dot access
The `new` binding, which takes precedence over implicit binding even though a dot is present
Default binding, since no object is explicitly passed
Explicit binding, because `fn` is a property lookup
mcqs.explanation: `new` outranks implicit binding in the precedence order: when a function is invoked with `new`, `this` is always the newly constructed object, regardless of what object the function happened to be accessed through. The dot here only finds the function; it doesn't participate in the call once `new` is involved.

mcqs.question: Why does `arrowFn.call(someObject)` fail to change what `this` refers to inside `arrowFn`?
options: `call` only works on functions declared with the `function` keyword, and silently no-ops otherwise
Arrow functions throw a TypeError whenever `.call()` is used on them
Arrow functions don't have their own `this` binding to overwrite — theirs is resolved lexically from the enclosing scope, so `call`'s argument is ignored
`this` inside an arrow function is always the global object regardless of how it's called
mcqs.explanation: Arrow functions opt out of the four binding rules entirely — there's no `this` slot for `call`/`apply`/`bind` to set, so the argument is silently ignored rather than throwing. What `this` resolves to instead depends entirely on the enclosing non-arrow scope, not on being global by default.

options: `setTimeout` cannot accept class methods as callbacks under any circumstances
`this.seconds` was never initialized because the constructor ran asynchronously
Class methods are read-only and `+=` mutates a frozen property
`setTimeout` calls `t.tick` bare, detached from `t`, so `this` inside `tick` is `undefined` in strict mode
mcqs.explanation: Passing `t.tick` extracts the function itself, severing its connection to `t` — when `setTimeout` eventually invokes it, it's a bare call, so `this` is `undefined` in strict mode and `this.seconds` throws. The constructor runs synchronously at `new Timer()` and class methods aren't frozen; the bug is purely about the detached call.

mcqs.question: Fixing the `Timer` bug with `this.tick = this.tick.bind(this)` in the constructor — what does this actually do?
options: It creates a new function, permanently locked to this instance's `this`, and assigns it onto the instance, shadowing the prototype method for callback use
It modifies the original `tick` method on the prototype so all instances share the fix
It converts `tick` into an arrow function at runtime
It defers `tick`'s execution until the next microtask
mcqs.explanation: `bind` returns a brand-new bound function; assigning it to `this.tick` creates an own property on the instance that shadows the prototype's `tick` whenever accessed via that instance. The prototype method itself is untouched — other instances calling `.bind` independently get their own bound copies, not a shared fix.

undefined, because `setTimeout` invokes the callback bare, so `this` isn't `app` inside it
A ReferenceError, because `this` is undefined inside `setTimeout`
